data.authority: ISO 26262-5:2018, Road vehicles — Functional safety — Part 5: Product development at the hardware level ([Kekaoxing][1])
data.calculation: ISO 26262 single-point fault metric (SPFM)
data.clause_locator: Annex C for the metric calculation; Clause 8.4.5 and Table 4 for quantitative target values
data.formula_or_test: SPFM = 1 - [Σ(λ_SPF + λ_RF) / Σλ_SR,HW], equivalently the fraction of the total safety-related hardware failure rate remaining after excluding single-point and residual faults. The compliance test is SPFM ≥ 90% for ASIL B, ≥ 97% for ASIL C, and ≥ 99% for ASIL D.
inputs: λ_SR,HW: total failure rates of safety-related hardware elements

data.clause_locator: Annex C for the metric calculation; Clause 8.4.6 and Table 5 for quantitative target values
data.formula_or_test: LFM = 1 - [Σλ_MPF,latent / Σ(λ_SR,HW - λ_SPF - λ_RF)]. The compliance test is LFM ≥ 60% for ASIL B, ≥ 80% for ASIL C, and ≥ 90% for ASIL D.
inputs: λ_SR,HW: total safety-related hardware failure rates

data.authority: JEDEC JESD85A:2021, Methods for Calculating Failure Rates in Units of FITs ([Scribd][2])
data.calculation: JEDEC constant-failure-rate FIT point estimate with Arrhenius acceleration
data.formula_or_test: For the single-activation-energy case: AF = exp[(E_A/k)(1/T_USE - 1/T_STRESS)]; FIT_POINT = f × 10^9 / (t × ss × AF). Here f is observed failures, t is stress-test hours per device, ss is sample size, E_A is activation energy in eV, k = 8.6×10^-5 eV/K in JESD85A's worked procedure, and temperatures are absolute kelvin.
data.publicly_retrievable: JEDEC standard is publicly retrievable; third-party copies are also available
data.volatility: Low to medium; revised periodically as JEDEC reliability methodology evolves

data.clause_locator: Clause 2, definition of Arrhenius equation; §5.2 for deriving/using acceleration factors
data.formula_or_test: A_T = exp[(-E_AA/k)(1/T_TEST - 1/T_SYSTEM)] = λ_TEST/λ_SYSTEM. JESD91A specifies k = 8.62×10^-5 eV/K and temperatures in kelvin.
inputs: E_AA: apparent activation energy in eV
failure rates at the two temperatures

data.direction_check: The DECISION direction is strongly consistent with the paper. The paper explicitly says Niagara takes a radically different approach from single/dual-thread optimization: it optimizes for multithreaded performance in commercial servers, uses 32 hardware threads, and exploits TLP to improve throughput and hide memory latency. It further describes the architecture as eight four-thread groups sharing single-issue pipelines, rather than as an ILP-oriented wide/out-of-order design. This is not a general-knowledge reversal; the draft captures the central architectural thesis of the paper.
missing_from_story: The power/performance-per-watt motivation is underrepresented. The paper explicitly discusses data-center power density, says simply lowering ILP-processor clock frequency sacrifices performance proportionally, and states an expected Niagara dissipation of about 60 W.

The architectural mechanism connecting the decision to the implementation should be made explicit: eight groups of four hardware threads share a single-issue SPARC pipeline, with fine-grained thread scheduling used to hide memory and pipeline stalls.

The memory-system consequence is important: supporting 32 threads requires a memory subsystem scaled for bandwidth, including a shared banked L2, crossbar, and four memory channels providing more than 20 Gbytes/s.
The workload characterization is more nuanced than simply "low ILP": Table 1 shows most listed server workloads as Low or Medium ILP and High TLP, but TPC-H is classified High ILP and High TLP.

The paper's mechanism is not merely "many threads hide memory latency"; it specifically relies on sharing relatively simple pipelines among threads, with zero-cycle thread switching within a four-thread group.
data.most_defensible_part: The decision itself: "Design Niagara to optimize for multithreaded throughput in a commercial server environment rather than for single- or dual-thread performance." This is essentially the paper's explicit thesis, including the 32-hardware-thread implementation and the TLP/throughput rationale.

objections.claim_attacked: alternatives_or_rejected: "Single-thread/ILP optimization (multiple instruction issue, out-of-order issue, aggressive branch prediction) and machines optimized for single-thread performance."
objections.objection: This is directionally faithful, and the paper explicitly contrasts Niagara with processors using multiple instruction issue, out-of-order issue, and aggressive branch prediction. However, "rejected" is stronger than the paper's framing: it presents the limitations of that approach and motivates a different design for commercial servers, rather than documenting a formal alternative-evaluation process. The paper also specifically contrasts an ILP-optimized SMP with an aggregation of simple cores on one die.

objections.claim_attacked: rationale: "Commercial server workloads are dominated by TLP"
objections.objection: The underlying claim is supported, but "dominated" is slightly stronger than the paper's wording. The paper says commercial server applications "tend to have large amounts of TLP" and Table 1 classifies the listed workloads as High TLP, while one benchmark, TPC-H, is also High ILP. A more precise formulation is that the target server workloads generally expose substantial TLP, making throughput-oriented execution effective.

objections.claim_attacked: outcome: "application performance is increased by improving throughput (total work across threads)"
objections.objection: This is sound as a design objective, but it should not be read as a quantified demonstrated outcome for every application. The paper explicitly defines the approach as improving application performance through throughput and says many multithreaded applications should realize performance improvements; it does not establish that every workload or single-thread application improves.

objections.claim_attacked: gaps: "The paper does not quantify the measured power or performance difference versus a specific single-thread ILP processor."
objections.objection: As phrased, this is incomplete. The paper does not provide a measured head-to-head power/performance comparison against a named ILP processor in the introduction, but it does give an explicit expected Niagara power figure of about 60 W and provides qualitative Figure 1 plus workload characterization in Table 1. Thus the gap should distinguish "no specific measured head-to-head comparison" from "no quantitative power figure."

objections.claim_attacked: gaps: "It does not state the target clock frequency for the thread-rich design."
objections.objection: This is not obviously a flaw in the episode, because the paper explicitly argues that TLP improves performance without pushing the envelope on CPU clock frequency, but the searched paper text does not expose a target-frequency number. The gap itself is therefore plausible; the stronger issue is that clock frequency is not central to the stated decision and should not be implied to be an omitted quantitative decision criterion.

objections.claim_attacked: gaps: "It does not give quantitative ILP-vs-TLP performance comparisons, only a qualitative figure and Table 1 (application ILP/TLP categories)."
objections.objection: This is broadly accurate for the cited introduction. Figure 1 is explicitly schematic/qualitative, and Table 1 gives Low/Medium/High classifications rather than performance numbers. However, the wording "does not give quantitative ILP-vs-TLP performance comparisons" should not be generalized to the entire nine-page paper without checking all later evaluation material. The paper is an architecture description and includes additional implementation/performance discussion beyond the introduction.

objections.claim_attacked: rationale: "Diminishing returns from single-thread focus because of limits to latency to main memory and inherently low ILP of applications"
objections.objection: This is particularly well grounded. The paper directly attributes diminishing returns to main-memory latency and inherently low ILP, and later explains low ILP through large working sets, poor locality, difficult data-dependent branches, and load-load dependencies.

data.quote_plausibility: Highly plausible and, based on the retrieved paper text, appears to be verbatim paper prose rather than a paraphrase dressed as a quote. The sentence occurs in the introduction with the same wording and is immediately followed by the discussion of commercial server applications and TLP.

data.answer: No: the four observed factors are not exactly mutually consistent with one uniform factor, and they are not exactly 1.049000. The first three are consistent with an underlying factor near 1.049304 after whole-dollar rounding; Tier D's small-dollar rounding makes its implied factor noticeably less reliable.
data.steps: Tier A: 130461 / 124331 = 1.0493038743354433, so to 6 decimals = 1.049304; implied percentage increase = (1.0493038743354433 - 1) × 100 = 4.9303874335%. Tier B: 3914 / 3730 = 1.0493297587131367, so to 6 decimals = 1.049330; implied increase = 4.9329758713%. Tier C: 26092 / 24866 = 1.0493042708919810, so to 6 decimals = 1.049304; implied increase = 4.9304270892%. Tier D: 1305 / 1243 = 1.0498793242156075, so to 6 decimals = 1.049879; implied increase = 4.9879324216%. The factors are not exactly identical, so the displayed dollar values are not mutually consistent with one single rounded 4.9% multiplier. The first three are tightly clustered around 1.049304 (about 4.9304%), while Tier D is materially higher at about 4.9879%. This is consistent with the official explanation that the 4.9% is the rounded CPI-U percentage and that the resulting thresholds are rounded to whole dollars; the underlying CPI index ratio, rather than exactly 1.049, therefore governs the calculations. The CFPB expressly says the 2024 adjustment reflects a 4.9% CPI-U increase and is rounded to whole dollars. ([Federal Register Public Inspection][1])

Infer the operational rounding rule as nearest whole dollar: the CFPB states that annual Regulation Z thresholds are adjusted using the CPI index and the resulting adjustment is rounded to whole dollars for ease of compliance. Tier A: 130461 × 1.034 = 130461 + (130461 × 0.034) = 130461 + 4435.674 = 134896.674; nearest whole dollar = $134,897. Tier B: 3914 × 1.034 = 3914 + (3914 × 0.034) = 3914 + 133.076 = 4047.076; nearest whole dollar = $4,047. Tier C: 26092 × 1.034 = 26092 + (26092 × 0.034) = 26092 + 887.128 = 26979.128; nearest whole dollar = $26,979. Tier D: 1305 × 1.034 = 1305 + (1305 × 0.034) = 1305 + 44.37 = 1349.37; nearest whole dollar = $1,349. The official 2025 rule indeed describes the adjustment as reflecting a 3.4% CPI-U increase. ([Consumer Financial Protection Bureau][2])

data.answer: The projection is $134,897 versus the official $134,841, an overstatement of $56. The exact factor is 1.033573251776393 (3.3573251776%), which is 4.2674822 basis points below the stated 3.4%.
data.steps: Official Tier A = $134,841. Projection = $134,897. Difference = 134897 - 134841 = $56, so the projection is $56 too high. Exact multiplier required to transform the 2024 value into the official 2025 value: 134841 / 130461 = 1.033573251776393. Exact percentage increase = (1.033573251776393 - 1) × 100 = 3.357325177639292%. Difference from the stated 3.4% = 3.357325177639292% - 3.4% = -0.042674822360708 percentage points. In basis points, -0.042674822360708 × 100 = -4.2674822360708 basis points. Thus the exact factor producing the official value is 1.033573251776393, corresponding to a 3.3573251776% increase, which is 4.2674822 bp below 3.4%. The official 2025 Tier A threshold is $134,841 and the CFPB identifies the adjustment as a 3.4% CPI-U increase. ([Consumer Financial Protection Bureau][2])

data.answer: The strongest reason is factor precision: 3.4% is a rounded representation of the underlying CPI-U index change used by the CFPB. Using exactly 1.034 therefore does not reproduce the agency's calculation; the underlying CPI-U index ratio is 1.033573251776393 for Tier A.
data.steps: The 2024 rule provides the key mechanism: the CFPB says the adjustment reflects a 4.9% increase in CPI-U, but the actual adjustment is based on the CPI-U index in effect on June 1 and the resulting amount is rounded to whole dollars. Therefore, '3.4%' is a rounded public description of the underlying CPI-U index change, not necessarily an instruction to multiply the prior threshold by exactly 1.034. Applying exactly 1.034 to $130,461 gives $134,896.674, whereas the official result is $134,841. The implied exact factor is 1.033573251776393. The concrete mechanism is therefore the precision/vintage of the underlying CPI-U index ratio used by the CFPB: the published 3.4% is rounded, while the agency calculation uses the underlying index values before rounding the dollar threshold. ([Federal Register Public Inspection][1])

data.weakest_point: The projection treats the published 3.4% CPI-U change as an exact multiplier (1.034), but the CFPB's actual methodology uses the underlying CPI-U index values as of the specified reference dates and only then rounds the resulting dollar threshold to whole dollars. The 3.4% figure is rounded, so its displayed precision is insufficient to reproduce $134,841 exactly. ([Federal Register Public Inspection][1])

n1 (1e21): Integers with 21 or more digits use exponential notation with uppercase 'e' and an explicit plus sign for positive exponents ('1e+21').

n3 (0.000001 = 1e-6): Numbers in range 10^-6 <= x < 1 (where exponent >= -6) are formatted in standard decimal notation ('0.000001').

n5 (-0): Negative zero is serialized as '0' (without negative sign per ES6 ToString).
n6 (333333333.33333329): Rounded to nearest IEEE 754 64-bit double precision representation, yielding shortest representation '333333333.3333333'.

data.direction_check: Verdict: direction matches recalled Niagara. This reads like the actual Niagara decision—many simple hardware threads to hide memory latency and raise commercial-server throughput—not a reversal and not a generic many-cores transplant. Recalled evidence, labeled as such: UltraSPARC T1/Niagara is remembered as an 8-core, 4-threads-per-core in-order chip with 32 hardware threads, favoring throughput and power efficiency over aggressive single-thread OoO/ILP. Exact page/table/page-number claims remain cannot-judge-without-the-paper.
missing_from_story: The structural decomposition behind "32 threads": recalled as 8 cores × 4 threads per core, not 32 full cores.
The pipeline implication: simple/in-order issue per core with multithreading to hide latency, rather than wide OoO issue.
The memory-hierarchy motivation: shared on-chip L2 and on-chip memory-controller rationale for avoiding main-memory latency; exact capacities are cannot-judge-without-the-paper.
First-order power/performance-per-watt constraint and process/frequency/area targets; treat exact values as must-verify rather than asserted.
Workload evidence: OLTP/web/Java-style commercial server behavior and why throughput, not lowest single-request latency, is the metric.
The tradeoff admission: high thread count can reduce per-thread performance and complicate cache/memory bandwidth; the win is conditional on enough concurrent threads.
data.most_defensible_part: The decision/rationale core is the keep-unchanged element: choose thread-rich throughput to hide memory latency because single-thread ILP returns are diminishing and commercial server load is embarrassingly parallel across requests. The direct quote also plausibly supports exactly that throughput definition, subject to source-byte verification.

objections.claim_attacked: outcome: "application performance is increased by improving throughput"
objections.objection: Mechanistically this overgeneralizes. Niagara's claim is about aggregate throughput for TLP-rich commercial workloads; it does not imply faster single-request latency or universal application speedup. Correct version: total work per unit time across many hardware threads rises, while per-thread performance may be modest and single-thread ILP is explicitly not the goal. Recalled-plausibility, not paper-verified.

objections.claim_attacked: rationale: "commercial server workloads are dominated by TLP"
objections.objection: The mechanism is directionally right but phrased too absolutely. The stronger claim is that commercial servers run many concurrent transactions/requests that expose thread- or request-level parallelism, while each thread still stalls on memory; therefore throughput scaling across threads pays off. "Dominated by TLP" can be misread as every program has high ILP/TLP internally. Recalled-plausibility.

objections.claim_attacked: alternatives_or_rejected: "simply running ILP processors at lower clock frequencies to save power"
objections.objection: The ILP-versus-thread-rich contrast is plausible, but this exact alternative sounds like an inferred foil rather than a cleanly stated rejected design point. A correct version would separate: rejected complexity/power of aggressive OoO/superscalar ILP; rejected single-thread optimization as the primary goal; and the power motivation for many simple cores. Whether the paper names "lower-clock ILP" as its own rejected option is cannot-judge-without-the-paper.

objections.claim_attacked: confidence: 0.95 despite gaps list omitting target clock and measured power/performance comparisons
objections.objection: Calibration objection rather than a paper-content claim: for a blind pre-screen of a design-decision episode, 0.95 is too high when the quantitative anchor (clock/power/perf-delta versus an ILP baseline) is absent from the story. Keep the direction, lower confidence or mark the missing numbers as must-verify for expert review.

data.quote_plausibility: High but still recalled-plausibility. The sentence is a complete definitional appositive—"throughput, the total amount of work done across multiple threads of execution"—which sounds like IEEE Micro introduction prose rather than a generic paraphrase: specific, short, and explanatory rather than ornamental. I cannot byte-verify the source line without the paper, and any source line-wrap normalization should be disclosed outside the quote string.

data.steps: The stated 3.4% is a one-decimal-place headline rounding. Applying 3.4% instead of 3.357% to the $130,461 base introduces $130461×0.000427 ≈ $56 of overshoot, which is exactly the observed discrepancy. data.answer: Implied 2023->2024 factors: A 1.049304, B 1.049330, C 1.049304, D 1.049879. The raw per-tier ratios are not identical, so they are not mutually consistent with one exact uniform factor applied independently to each tier. A and C match to six decimals; B is slightly higher; D is higher because small-dollar rounding has a larger proportional effect. A literal 4.9% factor is 1.049000, which is below all four implied ratios, so 4.9% is a rounded description rather than the exact factor. The 2024 values also show that B, C, and D equal rounded 3%, 20%, and 1% of tier A, respectively, so the official structure can still be driven by a single tier-A adjustment factor plus percentage-derived rounding.

Projected 2025 values using 3.4% and nearest-dollar rounding: tier A $134,897; tier B $4,047; tier C floor $26,979; tier D $1,349. If B/C/D are recomputed from the rounded projected tier A as 3%, 20%, and 1%, the results are the same: B = round(0.03 * 134897) = round(4046.91) = 4047; C = round(0.20 * 134897) = round(26979.4) = 26979; D = round(0.01 * 134897) = round(1348.97) = 1349.

The projection of $134,897 is $56 higher than the official $134,841. The exact factor that would produce $134,841 from $130,461 is approximately 1.033573252. That is 4.27 basis points lower than the nominal 3.4% factor of 1.034000.

Exact factor that produces official A from 2024 A = 134841 / 130461 = 1 + 4380/130461.
4380/130461 = 0.0335732518..., so exact factor = 1.0335732518...
Stated 3.4% factor = 1.034000.
Difference = 1.0335732518 - 1.034000 = -0.0004267482.
Basis-point discrepancy = -0.0004267482 * 10000 = -4.267482 bp.

n4=100000000000000000000: large integer within safe range serialized as decimal integer with no exponential notation — '100000000000000000000'
n5=-0: JCS distinguishes -0 from +0; serialized as '-0.0' (minus sign preserved, with '.0')
n6=333333333.33333329: exact value representable, serialized as decimal '333333333.33333329' (no exponent)
Key sort: all keys 'n1'..'n6' already in order; JCS key sorting by UTF-16 code units: 'n1'<n2'<...<'n6'
JCS key sort uses UTF-16 code-unit (binary) comparison, NOT Unicode code-point or locale
Code-unit values of lead surrogates: '$' U+0024 (36), 'a' U+0061 (97), 'ü' U+00FC (252) — but in UTF-16 'ü' is one 16-bit code unit 0x00FC
€ (U+20AC) in UTF-16 is code unit 0x20AC (8396)
Order by UTF-16 code units: 0x0024 ('$') < 0x0061 ('a') < 0x00FC ('ü') < 0x20AC ('€')
Thus JCS order: '$', 'aa', 'ü', '€'
Compact kept insertion order: €, $, ü, aa
JCS strings use minimal escape per JSON/JavaScript: \n for U+000A, \t for U+0009, \" for U+0022
s1: line feed (U+000A) escaped as \n
s2: tab (U+0009) escaped as \t
s3: double quote (U+0022) escaped as \"
s4: 'é' (U+00E9) is a printable non-ASCII character — JCS does NOT escape it; kept as literal UTF-8 'é'

s5: trailing spaces — JCS does not escape regular space (U+0020); BUT a single trailing space before closing quote: if string ends with a space, JCS per RFC 8785 does NOT escape it — kept as literal space

data.answer: The single strongest mechanism: the regulator does not apply the rounded, publicly-announced headline percentage (e.g., '3.4 percent') directly to the prior year's already-rounded dollar figure. Internally the adjustment is computed from a full-precision CPI-U index ratio (specific reference month/vintage, unrounded), applied to an unrounded (or differently-rounded) base, and only the FINAL result is rounded to the nearest dollar. The publicly stated 'X.X percent' is itself a rounded summary of that index ratio, not the exact multiplier used in the calculation. This explains both observations here: (1) in Task 1, the four 2023->2024 tiers do not share one exact factor even though they presumably derive from a single CPI-U ratio — because each tier's PRIOR-year rounded dollar value interacts differently with rounding, and the smallest base (Tier D) shows the largest deviation (57.5 bps) since rounding noise is proportionally largest there; (2) in Task 3, applying the rounded '3.4 percent' headline to the rounded 2024 Tier A value misses the official 2025 figure by $56 (~4.3 bps), because the true multiplier was ~3.3573%, not exactly 3.4000%.

DAL A and B additionally invoke DO-254 Appendix B advanced verification (elemental analysis, safety-specific analysis, formal methods, architectural mitigation); DAL A must justify coverage targets. NOTE: objective counts widely circulated on vendor sites as A=71, B=69, C=62, D=26 are the DO-178C software counts — I could not verify any DO-254 objective count against the primary text (a FAA job-aid breakdown organizes DO-254 objectives into Appendix B Tables B-1..B-4, ~31-35 objectives). Do not encode counts without checking.
inputs: item vs functional DAL (IDAL vs FDAL)
whether AC 20-152A or EASA AMC 20-152A applies
data.publicly_retrievable: partly free — DO-254 itself is paywalled (RTCA/EUROCAE store); AC 20-152A is a free FAA PDF and restates scope, DAL A/B/C applicability and the DAL D relief
data.volatility: static since 2000; DO-254A in preparation, and AC 20-152A (2022) materially expanded the applicable objective set

data.authority: RTCA DO-254 / EUROCAE ED-80, Design Assurance Guidance for Airborne Electronic Hardware, paragraph 1.6 ('Complexity considerations'), as quoted verbatim in FAA Order 8110.105A, Chapter 1 (definitions section)
data.calculation: DO-254 simple vs complex electronic hardware classification test (determines whether the full DO-254 life-cycle objective set applies)
data.clause_locator: DO-254 paragraph 1.6 (quoted verbatim as 'Source: RTCA/DO-254, paragraph 1.6' in FAA Order 8110.105A)
data.formula_or_test: Test: an item is SIMPLE iff a comprehensive combination of deterministic tests and analyses appropriate to the design assurance level ensures correct functional performance under all foreseeable operating conditions with no anomalous behavior. If the item is not simple, it is COMPLEX (complex hardware item = all items that are not simple) and the full DO-254 life cycle applies; a collection of simple items may itself be complex, and a device containing an ASIC or PLD can still be simple if it meets the test. For complex items the proposed design-assurance method must be agreed with the certification authority early in the life cycle.
inputs: set of deterministic tests and analyses performed
design assurance level of the item
device type (ASIC/PLD/FPGA vs discrete), untestable modes, hidden states in state machines
data.publicly_retrievable: paywalled original, but the operative definition is reproduced verbatim in the free FAA Order 8110.105A PDF (faa.gov)
data.volatility: static since 2000

data.authority: Export Administration Regulations (EAR), 15 CFR parts 730-774, Commerce Control List Category 3 — Electronics, ECCN 3A090 (Supplement No. 1 to Part 774), as amended (notably the Oct 2022, Oct 17 2023, Dec 2024 and Feb 14 2025 BIS rules)
data.calculation: US export-control classification test for advanced computing integrated circuits: total processing performance (TPP) and performance density (PD) versus ECCN 3A090 thresholds
data.clause_locator: ECCN 3A090.a and 3A090.b, Technical Note 2 to 3A090.a and 3A090.b (TPP definition, items 1.a-1.d, 2, 3, 4), Technical Note 1 to 3A090.c; Notes 2-4 to 3A090.a and 3A090.b. Threshold text verified verbatim in 90 FR (Feb 14, 2025) FR Doc. 2025-02655 / BIS rule text.
data.formula_or_test: TPP = 2 x MacTOPS x (bit length of the operation), aggregated over all processing units: TPP = TPP1 + TPP2 + ... + TPPn. MacTOPS = theoretical peak 10^12 multiply-accumulate operations/second (D = A x B + C), taken at its maximum theoretically possible rate (highest value the manufacturer claims in manual/brochure); bit length of the operation = largest bit length of the inputs to the multiply operation; for chips supporting several bit lengths evaluate the HIGHEST TPP; for sparse+dense capable parts use the dense (no-sparsity) values. PD = TPP / applicable die area, area in mm^2 including all die area of logic dies made on a non-planar transistor architecture process node. Classification: 3A090.a if TPP >= 4800 OR (TPP >= 1600 AND PD >= 5.92); 3A090.b if (2400 <= TPP < 4800 AND 1.6 <= PD < 5.92) OR (TPP >= 1600 AND 3.2 <= PD < 5.92); 3A090.c covers HBM with memory bandwidth density > 2 GB/s/mm^2 (bandwidth in GB/s divided by package-or-stack area in mm^2). Carve-out: 3A090.a/b do not apply to items not designed or marketed for datacenters AND with TPP < 4800 (see license exceptions NAC and ACA).
inputs: MacTOPS per processing unit (peak, theoretical, per datasheet)
bit length of the multiply inputs per unit
applicable die area in mm^2 (non-planar logic dies)
whether designed or marketed for datacenter use
for 3A090.c: HBM bandwidth (GB/s) and package/stack area (mm^2)
data.publicly_retrievable: free (eCFR 15 CFR 774 Supp. No. 1; Federal Register at govinfo.gov; BIS bis.doc.gov PDFs)
data.volatility: high — thresholds and notes have been rewritten repeatedly (Oct 2022, Oct 2023, Dec 2024, Jan 2025 AI-diffusion rule later rescinded, Feb 2025); always pull current eCFR text

data.authority: Export Administration Regulations (EAR), 15 CFR 772.1 (definitions) — 'advanced-node integrated circuit'; related de minimis rule at 15 CFR 734.4(a)(3)
data.calculation: EAR 'advanced-node integrated circuit' definition test (triggers advanced-node SME/end-use controls and 0% de minimis for certain lithography equipment)
data.clause_locator: 15 CFR 772.1 (definition added by the Oct 17 2023 'Export Controls on Semiconductor Manufacturing Items' rule; 88 FR)
data.formula_or_test: An integrated circuit is an 'advanced-node integrated circuit' if ANY of: (1) logic IC using a non-planar transistor architecture OR with a production technology node of 16/14 nanometers or less; (2) NOT-AND (NAND) memory IC with 128 layers or more; (3) DRAM IC using a production technology node of 18 nanometer half-pitch or less. Related deterministic threshold (not verified against current eCFR text): 0% de minimis applies to certain lithography equipment in ECCN 3B001.f.1.b.2.b when destined for development or production of advanced-node ICs meeting criterion (1). NOTE: sourced from a law-firm summary of the Oct 17 2023 SME rule; later rules may have amended the definition — verify in 15 CFR 772.1 before use.
inputs: production technology node (nm) or DRAM half-pitch (nm)
data.volatility: high — definitions added/amended with each SME and advanced-computing rule package

data.authority: Internal Revenue Code section 48D (26 U.S.C. 48D), added by section 107(a) of the CHIPS Act of 2022 (Division A of Pub. L. 117-167); implemented by Treas. Reg. T.D. 10009 (26 CFR 1.48D-1 et seq., effective 2024-12-23)
data.calculation: CHIPS Act advanced manufacturing investment credit amount (US semiconductor fab / semiconductor manufacturing equipment investment tax credit)
data.clause_locator: IRC 48D(a) (25% rate), 48D(b)(1)-(5) (qualified investment/property/facility), 48D(c) (eligible taxpayer), 48D(d) (elective payment), 48D(e) (construction-begin deadline); CHIPS Act sec. 107(f)(1) (placed-in-service/post-2022-08-09 basis limitation)
data.formula_or_test: Credit = 25% x qualified investment for the taxable year with respect to an advanced manufacturing facility, where qualified investment = basis of qualified property placed in service during the year. Qualified property = tangible depreciable/amortizable property integral to the operation of the facility, constructed/reconstructed/erected by the taxpayer or acquired with original use commencing with the taxpayer (buildings and structural components qualify unless used for offices/administrative or other non-manufacturing functions). Conditions: property must be placed in service after 2022-12-31; for construction begun before 2023-01-01 only the basis attributable to construction after 2022-08-09 counts; no credit for property whose construction begins after 2026-12-31 (sunset). IRS guidance states the rate is 25% for property placed in service through 2025-12-31 and 35% for property placed in service thereafter (attributed by IRS to the Working Families Tax Cuts Act of 2025; a trade source calls the same change the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — name not independently verified). Treasury regs add a >50% test for 'primary purpose' (final regs T.D. 10009).
inputs: tax basis of each qualified property
portion of basis attributable to construction after 2022-08-09 (if pre-2023 start)
whether property is integral to semiconductor or semiconductor-equipment manufacturing
whether taxpayer is a foreign entity of concern / made an applicable transaction under IRC 50(a)
election to treat credit as a payment of tax (IRC 48D(d))
data.publicly_retrievable: free (IRS.gov credit page; govinfo for T.D. 10009 and Pub. L. 117-167; 26 U.S.C. 48D on uscode.house.gov/LII)
data.volatility: low for the statutory 25%; medium for the rate/termination dates (the 2025 reconciliation act raised the post-2025 rate to 35% and bipartisan bills would extend the 2026 sunset)

data.authority: 15 CFR 231.108 (CHIPS Program, NIST, 'Preventing the Improper Use of CHIPS Act Funding'), issued under 15 U.S.C. 4651 et seq.; prohibition at 15 CFR 231.202; notification at 15 CFR 231.301-231.303
data.calculation: CHIPS guardrails 'material expansion' test — whether a planned expansion of semiconductor manufacturing capacity in a foreign country of concern triggers the Expansion Clawback / notification duty
data.clause_locator: 15 CFR 231.108 ('Material expansion.'), as revised at 88 FR 89574, Dec. 28, 2023 (also printed at 88 FR 61614/65600, Sept. 2023 final rule)
data.formula_or_test: Material expansion means: (1) with respect to an existing facility, an increase of the semiconductor manufacturing capacity of that facility by MORE THAN FIVE PERCENT of the capacity memorialized in the required agreement, due to addition of a cleanroom, production line or other physical space (or a series of such additions); OR (2) any construction of a new facility for semiconductor manufacturing. Test: delta_capacity / capacity_memorialized_in_agreement > 0.05 -> material expansion; new facility -> material expansion per se. Consequence: during the 10-year period from the award date, a covered entity (and its affiliated group, per 26 U.S.C. 1504 80% ownership) may not engage in a significant transaction involving material expansion in a foreign country of concern, with narrow exceptions for existing legacy-semiconductor facilities and for legacy capacity predominantly serving the market of that country; notification to notifications@chips.gov required regardless; remedy can be recovery of the full award. Secondary-source caveats (NOT verified against eCFR): a 10% capacity threshold is applied to legacy-semiconductor facilities, 'significant transaction' is commonly cited as >= $100,000, and the legacy exception is cited as >=85% of output consumed in the country of concern.
inputs: capacity memorialized in the required agreement (baseline)
planned incremental capacity from the addition
whether the addition is a cleanroom/production line/physical space
whether a new facility is being constructed
legacy vs non-legacy semiconductor classification (28nm-or-older logic, DRAM >18nm half-pitch, NAND <128 layers, wafer size, packaging technology)
country of concern status (China, Russia, Iran, North Korea per 10 U.S.C. 4872(d))
data.publicly_retrievable: free (eCFR; Federal Register at govinfo.gov; NIST CHIPS FAQ page)
data.volatility: medium — definition revised once already (Dec 2023) and guardrails are politically live; verify current eCFR and any amended required agreement

data.authority: JEDEC JESD85 (JESD85A), Methods for Calculating Failure Rates in Units of FITs
data.calculation: JEDEC FIT (failures in time) rate from accelerated life-test data, including the upper-confidence-bound chi-square estimator
data.formula_or_test: 1 FIT = 1 failure per 10^9 device-hours. Point estimate: FIT = (number of failures f) x 10^9 / (N x H x AF). Upper-confidence-bound form used in qualification reports: FIT_CL = chi2(CL, 2f+2) x 10^9 / (2 x N x H x AF), where N = number of units on test, H = test hours, AF = acceleration factor; for f = 0 and CL = 60%, chi2(60%, 2)/2 = 0.92 (i.e. chi2 = 1.833). Worked industry example: 231 units x 1000 h, 0 failures, AF = 259 -> FIT ~= 1.833e9 / (2 x 231 x 1000 x 259) = 15.3 FIT at 60% CL. MTTF(hours) = 10^9 / FIT. NOTE: the chi-square estimator and its 60% CL convention are the form published in JEDEC-member qualification reports attributed to JESD85; I have not read JESD85 itself, so the section numbering and exact CL defaults are unverified.
inputs: confidence level CL (60% typical industrial, 90%/95% stricter)
data.publicly_retrievable: paywalled (JEDEC store); the applied formula is reproduced in many free vendor qualification reports/datasheets (e.g. AOS reliability reports)
data.volatility: static (method stable; revision letters JESD85 -> JESD85A)

data.authority: JEDEC JESD47 (Stress-Test-Driven Qualification of Integrated Circuits, e.g. JESD47K) with the HTOL stress method in JEDEC JESD22-A108 (Temperature, Bias, and Operating Life, e.g. JESD22-A108F)
data.calculation: JEDEC stress-test-driven qualification of integrated circuits: HTOL (high-temperature operating life) pass/fail test and sample-size rule
data.formula_or_test: Qualification test: stress sample at junction temperature Tj >= 125 C (JESD22-A108 sets ambient/chamber conditions, +/-5 C tolerance) with Vcc >= Vccmax (max operating voltage up to absolute maximum rating), for 1000 hours, with readpoints typically at 168 / 500 / 1000 h. Sample size: 3 non-consecutive lots x 77 units each = 231 units (LTPD-based sampling, JESD47). Acceptance criterion: 0 failures at 1000 h. The 0/231 result is then converted to a FIT number via JESD85 with an Arrhenius AF (see JEP122 entry).
inputs: junction temperature during stress (K or C)
stress voltage vs Vccmax / absolute max
use-condition junction temperature and Ea for the FIT conversion
data.publicly_retrievable: paywalled (JEDEC store); values widely reproduced in free vendor qualification reports and reliability-appnote PDFs
data.volatility: low — 1000 h / 125 C / 77 x 3 / 0-fail convention has been stable for decades; automotive overlays (AEC-Q100) add stricter conditions

data.authority: JEDEC publication JEP122 (Failure Mechanisms and Models for Semiconductor Devices); first-order activation-energy table reproduced in NASA NEPP SSB-1, Guidelines for Using Plastic Encapsulated Microcircuits (citing EIA/JEP122)
data.calculation: JEDEC thermal acceleration factor (Arrhenius) and activation-energy selection for converting accelerated test time to use-condition life; plus Black's equation for electromigration
data.formula_or_test: Arrhenius: Rate = A0  exp(-Ea/kT) (equivalently exp(Ea/kT) form for time-to-fail), k = 8.617e-5 eV/K. Thermal acceleration factor: AF = exp[(Ea/k) x (1/T_use - 1/T_stress)] with T in kelvin. Field-equivalent hours = test hours x AF; equivalently lambda_use = lambda_stress / AF. Ea selection (first-order JEP122 table as reproduced in NASA NEPP SSB-1): surface/oxide 1.0 eV; charge loss (dynamic memory) 0.6; dielectric breakdown field >0.04 micron 0.3, field <=0.04 micron 0.7; metallization electromigration (Al and Al alloys) 0.6; corrosion with chlorine 0.70, with phosphorus 0.53; chemical contamination 1.00; silicon/crystal defects 0.50. A second widely used JEP122-derived table gives EM activation energies of ~0.48-0.72 eV by metallurgy (AlCu ~0.70) and TDDB ~0.3 (thin) / ~0.7 (thick). Industry default when the mechanism is unknown: Ea = 0.7 eV (e.g., 1000 h at 125 C vs 55 C use -> AF ~259). Electromigration (Black): MTTF = A  J^(-n) * exp(Ea/kT), with current-density exponent n typically taken as 2 (reported range 1-2) and Cu-damascene Ea ~0.8-1.0 eV vs Al ~0.5-0.7 eV. NOTE: Ea tables differ between JEP122 editions/secondary reproductions — pick the edition you cite.
inputs: activation energy Ea (eV) for the dominant failure mechanism
for EM: current density J, exponent n, metallization type
data.publicly_retrievable: paywalled (JEDEC store — check whether the specific JEP122 revision is a free download); the first-order Ea table is reproduced free in the NASA NEPP SSB-1 PDF
data.volatility: low-medium — stable physics; edition-to-edition Ea tables and Cu-vs-Al values shift with new metallization data

data.attribution_check: Attribution is present and largely clean, with three gaps. Present: a named participant (eder-matheus, flagged MEMBER), a date (2024-11-14), and a locator (the issue URL). Does it support the claim chosen_intervention attaches to it? Only partly. (1) The quoted span covers just the layer-adjustment half - 'we could finish GRT by changing the routing layer adjustments from 0.45 to 0.2' - while the 'congestion iterations to 35' half that chosen_intervention also asserts sits outside the quoted text, so that clause is currently unquoted. (2) The verb is 'could': the quote evidences a capability or a successful experiment, which supports the letter of chosen_intervention but not post_state's implication of resolution. (3) The locator is the thread URL, not a comment permalink, so the quote cannot be byte-checked against a specific comment - worth tightening since this is the one element that is verifiable in-paste. Also: the record never states eder-matheus's role beyond MEMBER or whether they personally ran the experiment, and the ~2024-11-14 quote sits about a year and a half before the 2026 stale closure with no confirming update in between.
data.evidence_check: post_state is asserted, not measured - it rests entirely on a participant's sentence, not on a rerun. What was actually reported: that GRT 'could finish' / that the change was made 'to complete BoomTile'. What was never reported: the post-fix congestion DRC count (baseline was 20k - the one number that would settle the episode), total and per-layer overflow before/after, runtime, whether the run reproduced, whether detailed routing and final DRC/timing were ever reached, and whether the change was committed to a flow/platform script or applied only locally. A closed-out fix would have to show: the same repro script rerun end-to-end, before/after DRC and overflow numbers, runtime cost, and confirmation that the design subsequently passes detailed route and signoff DRC - GRT completion alone is not that. Note also that auto-closure as not_planned/Stale is not evidence of a fix and cuts mildly against the change having been adopted anywhere.
data.mechanism_check: Partially holds, and breaks at the load-bearing step. The chain I can believe: GRT's congestion model derates per-layer capacity by the adjustment; with 0.45 inherited from other asap7 designs, the model is pessimistic for this design's layer stack, so the router flags overflow, iterates, and with the default 30-iteration budget either exits or stalls, leaving 20k congestion markers; lowering the adjustment to 0.2 and granting 35 iterations lets the run reach completion. Where it breaks: (i) the sign of the adjustment is never fixed in the record, so the step '0.45 too aggressive -> 0.2 relieves congestion' is asserted, not derived (see objection 4); (ii) both the symptom (localized top-of-die and around-macro region) and the record's own named alternative cause (a path looping around the macro, #5971) are local/topological, while both knobs are global - a global derate cannot remove a detour path, it can only change what gets flagged or let the run terminate; (iii) 'finish GRT' is a termination claim, not a cleanliness claim, and no post-fix count exists to bridge them; (iv) the 30 -> 35 delta is too small to be the operative change if 30 was truly insufficient, which leaves the adjustment doing all the work - or leaves completion explained by something else entirely. Net: the mechanism is coherent as 'the router stopped erroring under a different capacity model' and not coherent as 'the congestion was fixed'. With two knobs moved together, no single-parameter attribution is possible from this record.
missing_from_story: Scope of the fix: whether 0.45 -> 0.2 was applied to BoomTile alone or to the shared asap7 platform - the hypothesis says 0.45 was 'originally derived from other asap7 designs', so a platform-level change carries regression exposure for those designs and is a flow-policy decision, not just a local workaround.

Which metal layers the adjustment applies to: the record says 'layer adjustments' without naming a single layer, and with a top-of-die hotspot the specific layer stack (and whether values are per-layer) is decisive.
What the 20k actually counts: GRT overflow markers versus real DRCs, and which report or log the number came from - 'congestion DRC' is used as if self-defining.
Whether the design was ever taken past GRT to detailed route, final DRC and timing after the parameter change; GRT completion is not signoff.
The outcome of the iteration sweep the record says was performed - which values were tried and what happened at each.
Runtime and QoR cost: what 35 iterations cost in wall-clock, and what a lower layer adjustment costs later in routability or timing.

A structural account of the top-of-die hot region (macro placement, halo/blockage, pin access, PDN stripes, IO ring) - the record offers only the looping-path hypothesis and defers even that to #5971.

Who filed the issue and on exactly what invocation: the repro script and ORFS commit are given, but not the reporter, the platform/asap7 revision, or whether other designs on the same flow showed the same behaviour.
The disposition of #5971, which the record itself names as the likely real root cause and which is expressly unresolved here.
data.most_defensible_part: The direct_quote object exactly as stored - text, by (eder-matheus, MEMBER), date (2024-11-14) and locator. It is verbatim-consistent with the parameter change reported in chosen_intervention, it is attributed to a named participant with a date and a locator, and it is the only element in the draft that can be checked against the pasted record at all, since the mechanism and the outcome both rest on things the thread never measured. Keep it unchanged; the only refinement is a reading note, not an edit: the quote evidences 'this parameter change let GRT finish', not 'the congestion was fixed', and it should be cited only for the former.

objections.claim_attacked: prior_state + observation, i.e. the incident's central framing: 'placement density was only 0.24 with a lot of open space, especially at the top of the die' set against 'Congestion heatmap shows a large region at the top of the die and around the macro'.
objections.objection: The record places the worst congestion in the emptiest part of the die and never reconciles it, leaving the title's paradox (20k congestion DRCs at 0.24 density) unexplained rather than resolved. Two branches, and both cut into the current story: (a) if the open top area really is free, then a hotspot there has a topological cause - the looping global-route path around the macro that the record itself defers to #5971 - and no global capacity knob should clear it; (b) if that area is in fact unusable (macro halo/blockage, stripes, pin access), then 0.24 is a misleading die-wide average and the 'plenty of room' premise collapses, because the design is locally dense exactly where it matters. The episode asserts the paradox as established fact without determining which branch holds, so its headline number is doing work it has not earned.

objections.claim_attacked: chosen_intervention -> post_state: that a global routing-layer capacity adjustment plus a global iteration budget resolved a localized congestion failure.
objections.objection: Symptom and remedy are mismatched in scale. The observation is a bounded hot region (top of die, around one macro); both knobs are chip-global. A global derate should shift reported overflow everywhere or nowhere, not selectively clear one local region, and a bigger iteration budget only lets the router keep trying - it does not remove a detour path. The record's own competing cause (a path 'looping around the macro' many times, #5971) is precisely the kind of local topology defect that a global parameter will not remove; it would only let GRT terminate. So the defensible reading of 'could finish GRT' is that the run stopped erroring/overflow-flagging, not that the 20k congestion DRCs were eliminated. The mechanism is coherent as 'tool completed', incoherent as 'congestion fixed'.

objections.claim_attacked: hypothesis, 'the default 30 congestion iterations were also insufficient', remedied by setting them to 35 - inside a change that simultaneously moved the layer adjustment 0.45 -> 0.2.
objections.objection: Two defects in one number. First, magnitude: 30 -> 35 is a 17% bump; if 30 iterations were genuinely insufficient as a causal factor, a 5-step increase is an implausibly small remedy, and the record also says iteration count was 'asked early on and swept' - a sweep would presumably have covered values above 30, so either the sweep outcome was never reported in this thread or the iteration count is not the operative variable at all. Second, confounding: both parameters were changed in the same run, so nothing in the record attributes completion to either the adjustment change, the iteration change, or their combination. As written, chosen_intervention supports no single-knob claim, which also means the '30 was insufficient' half of the hypothesis is untested by the fix offered for it.

objections.claim_attacked: hypothesis, 'The GRT routing-layer adjustment of 0.45 ... is too aggressive for this design' -> reduce to 0.2.
objections.objection: The sign of the knob is asserted, never established. The episode treats 'aggressive' as self-explanatory and treats 0.2 as the relaxation, but the record never states whether a higher adjustment means more or less usable per-layer capacity - and the draft's own gaps[3] concedes the high-vs-low meaning is only 'explained in prose' (while simultaneously listing it as a gap, so that field is internally inconsistent too). This is load-bearing: if a higher value means more available capacity, then 0.45 -> 0.2 is a tightening, and 'GRT completes' would have to be explained by the router repairing or flagging less rather than by congestion being relieved - the mechanism story inverts and the current wording becomes actively misleading. I am not asserting either reading; I am flagging that the episode asserts a direction it does not define, and that this is the single factual question an expert reviewer must settle before anything else in the causal chain can be graded. Downgrade to minor if the thread elsewhere defines the direction: not-determinable-from-this-record.

objections.claim_attacked: post_state, 'GRT was reported to complete ... after reducing the layer adjustment to 0.2 and setting congestion iterations to 35', carried as the episode's resolution.
objections.objection: The source verb is conditional - 'we could finish GRT', 'to complete BoomTile' - which is a capability or experiment report, not a validated fix; and the record's own gap says the issue was auto-closed not_planned/Stale with no PR and no stated merge. Whether the change was applied to the shared asap7 flow script or only locally, and whether it was ever adopted at all, is not-determinable-from-this-record. The draft's hedging ('reported to', 'No re-measured DRC count was given') is accurate; the residual defect is promoting an unvalidated workaround to the resolution slot of the episode. Classified minor here because the absence of measurement is an evidence defect handled in evidence_check, not a second fatal.

objections.claim_attacked: confidence: 0.8
objections.objection: 0.8 reads as 'essentially settled', which the record does not support: no post-fix number, root cause deferred to #5971, the main knob's direction undefined, two parameters changed simultaneously with no attribution, no PR, auto-closed as stale. By its own contents the thread supports 'cause hypothesized, workaround reported by a maintainer, never measured' - roughly 0.5-0.6. 0.8 would only be defensible if scoped to fidelity of extraction from the thread, which the field does not state.

data.direction_check: Direction matches; not a reversal, not a general-knowledge transplant. RECALLED evidence (all hedged): Niagara / UltraSPARC T1 is known precisely for eight deliberately simple single-issue in-order cores, four fine-grained hardware threads each, 32 threads total, a modest clock (~1.2 GHz, recalled) versus the 2-3+ GHz out-of-order parts of the era, a shared multi-megabyte L2 behind a crossbar, and a target of commercial-server throughput (web/OLTP/app-server class) at a low power envelope — i.e. throughput computing, trading single-thread performance away, which is exactly what this episode records. A reversal would read 'adopt aggressive out-of-order/speculation for single-thread speed' or 'use 32 threads to accelerate one thread'; nothing here does that. The one number I can check blind is 32, and it matches the paper title verbatim. Cannot-judge-without-the-paper on whether the specific rejected alternatives appear on page 1.
missing_from_story: The decomposition and the simplicity of the core: eight cores x four threads (recalled), each core single-issue, in-order, short pipeline — the throughput comes from many simple cores, not from 32 threads on one wide core. Without this, 'many hardware threads' reads as a thread-count tweak rather than a microarchitecture reversal.

The thread-switch policy and the latency argument's other half: fine-grained switching to another ready thread on long-latency events (L1 miss / load stall), the Little's-law requirement for enough concurrent misses, and the bandwidth side of the bargain (shared L2, crossbar, high off-chip bandwidth). 'Threads hide memory latency' alone is not a complete mechanism.

What was traded away: per-thread performance is substantially worse than a contemporary ILP core, and the machine is a poor fit for single-threaded and floating-point/technical code — the recalled consequence being a single shared FPU for the chip (verify: I recall one FPU shared across all eight cores, with per-core FPUs arriving only in Niagara 2; treat as recall, not fact). This is the falsifiable content of 'instead of single-thread ILP'.

The workload set the decision is conditioned on — commercial server benchmarks of the SPECjbb / SPECweb / TPC-C-like OLTP and web/app-tier class. Without naming them, 'commercial server environment' is unfalsifiable boilerplate.

The clock/power design point itself: a deliberately modest frequency chosen against contemporary high-frequency out-of-order parts, plus process node, die size and power envelope if the paper states them. This is the same ground as the gaps[1] dispute and should be resolved one way or the other.

Whether the paper's support is qualitative (workload categorization only) or quantitative (simulation/RTL/early-silicon results, throughput-per-watt). The episode's gaps assert the former; the answer determines whether outcome can carry numbers at all.
data.most_defensible_part: The decision direction in decision as anchored by direct_quote — 'design for multithreaded throughput across 32 hardware threads rather than for single-thread ILP, because commercial server workloads are TLP-rich and ILP-poor' — is the one element I would keep unchanged: it matches the paper's known identity (32 threads, simple cores, commercial-server throughput, deliberately sacrificed single-thread performance), it is mechanically coherent with the memory-latency plus low-ILP rationale, and the quote supplies a real definitional anchor for 'throughput' rather than a restatement of it.

objections.claim_attacked: gaps[1]: 'It does not state the target clock frequency for the thread-rich design.'
objections.objection: RECALL (not assertion; no paper in hand): this paper carries a key-features/implementation table listing the operating frequency (~1.2 GHz, 90 nm, recalled) and a power envelope next to the core/thread counts. If so, this gap is false as written, and it is not a harmless miss: a gap that claims the absence of a stated number is the most falsifiable kind of claim in the record, and this one also undercuts gaps[0], because the paper's power objection to ILP is made concretely by choosing a deliberately modest clock rather than by asserting power concern abstractly. Escape: if the frequency appears only in a later implementation section as the expected/measured frequency of the fabricated part and never as a design target chosen for power, downgrade to minor and reword to 'does not present the clock choice as a target trade-off in the introduction.'

objections.claim_attacked: gaps[2]: 'only a qualitative figure and Table 1 (application ILP/TLP categories)' — element type and index.
objections.objection: RECALL: the ILP-versus-TLP characterization of commercial workloads reads to me as a figure (a quadrant-style plot contrasting ILP-rich technical code with TLP-rich commercial code), whereas a 'Table 1' in a IEEE Micro paper of this kind is typically the processor-features table — which is exactly where the frequency/power numbers of gaps[1] would live. The two gap fields therefore cannot both be right: either Table 1 is the ILP/TLP categorization (and gaps[1] needs rechecking) or it is the feature table (and gaps[2] is mislabeled). Element indices are mechanically checkable, so this is a cheap fix before expert review.

objections.claim_attacked: alternatives_or_rejected: 'Also rejected: simply running ILP processors at lower clock frequencies to save power.'
objections.objection: cannot-judge-without-the-paper. This is the most transplant-prone field in the episode. The argument itself is mechanically sound (lower f cuts throughput roughly proportionally while dynamic power falls less than proportionally once voltage headroom runs out), and it is directionally consistent with the paper — but my recall places it more firmly in the surrounding Sun throughput-computing material and the Niagara-2-era retelling than in this paper's introduction. Not calling it wrong; flagging that if the reviewer checks only page 1, this rejected alternative may not be attested there, which would make it a general-knowledge transplant into an otherwise quote-anchored episode.

objections.claim_attacked: outcome: 'Niagara supports 32 hardware threads in hardware; application performance is increased by improving throughput (total work across threads).'
objections.objection: The outcome is non-informative: it restates the decision and paraphrases the quote, so it records no state of the world that changed and would read identically had the machine never been built. Either the paper has a performance section (simulation/RTL or early-silicon numbers on the commercial workload set, plus a throughput-per-watt claim), in which case the outcome should carry at least one number, or it does not, in which case the outcome should say so explicitly instead of laundering the decision as a result. Related calibration note on confidence 0.95: defensible if it means 'extraction fidelity of direction plus quote', indefensible if read as 'the paper supplies quantitative support' — the episode's own gaps concede it does not.

data.quote_plausibility: Reads as this paper's own intro prose rather than a paraphrase dressed as a quote: definitional appositive construction ('throughput, the total amount of work done across multiple threads of execution'), complete sentence, roughly twenty words, neutral register, no paraphrase tells such as 'the authors argue' or hedging verbs. Two caveats. (1) Byte-verbatim: cannot-judge-without-the-paper — the real risk is not wording but truncation, since sentences of this shape in that literature typically continue with an adjunct ('...in a given amount of time', '...rather than reducing the time to complete a single task'); a cleanly truncated extract that still reads complete is the classic way a paraphrase passes as a quote. (2) Evidential weight: the sentence attests the goal (throughput as the performance metric), not the trade-off (rejecting single-thread ILP). It should not be leaned on as proof of the rejection half of the decision, and the draft does not currently lean on it that way.

data.answer: The published 3.4% is a CPI-U increase rounded to one decimal; the official dollar figures are computed from the unrounded index ratio (2024 actual 1.0493039 = 4.9304%, 2025 actual 1.0335733 = 3.3573%). Applying a rate rounded to the nearest 10 bp against a ~130,461 base injects up to +/-65 of error -- about 110x the +/-0.50 whole-dollar rounding error, which is the only other mechanism in play. That is precisely the size and direction of the observed miss (56 low = 4.27 bp). Remedy: never use the published rounded percentage; recompute factor = CPI-U(index month, year N) / CPI-U(index month, year N-1) at full precision and apply it to the cumulative base.
data.steps:
Candidate mechanisms sized against the observed 56 / 4.27 bp miss:
(a) Whole-dollar rounding convention: bounded at +/-0.50 per tier, i.e. <=0.04 bp on a 134k base. Observed miss is 56. RULED OUT -- too small by ~110x.
(b) Tier-C truncate vs round-nearest ambiguity: bounded at 1 and only affects tier C. RULED OUT for the tier A miss.
(c) Published-percentage precision: '3.4%' is a one-decimal rounding of the true CPI-U increase. A +/-5 bp error in a rate applied to 130,461 is +/-65. Observed miss 56 sits inside this band. MATCHES in both sign and magnitude, and the identical signature appears in the 2023->2024 step (stated 4.9%, actual 4.9304%, naive-1.049 error $38 on tier A).
(d) Index vintage / which 12-month CPI-U window is used: could shift the rate by tens of bp, so it is a real risk, but it cannot be the discriminator here because the stated 3.4% already rounds consistently to the official value -- no vintage change is needed to explain the data.
Strongest single mechanism: (c).

data.weakest_point: The 3.4% input is itself a rounded number -- a CPI-U increase published to one decimal -- while the official 2025 tier A was produced from the unrounded index ratio 1.0335733 (3.3573%). My projection inherits that rounding: a rate rounded to the nearest 10 bp, applied to a 130,461 base, moves the answer by up to about 65, and the observed miss is 56 low (4.27 bp). The corroborating signature is that the 2023->2024 step behaves identically (stated 4.9%, actual 4.9304%, naive-1.049 error 38 on tier A), so this is a systematic feature of using the headline percentage rather than the index ratio -- not a one-off. Whole-dollar rounding convention is bounded at +/-$0.50 and cannot explain any of it.

rules_applied: Key sort = ascending UTF-16 code-unit order (RFC 8785 §3.2.3), NOT locale/case-insensitive collation: "C"=0x0043 (67) < "a"=0x0061 (97) < "b"=0x0062 (98), so uppercase precedes lowercase
Comparison is per 16-bit code unit of the raw key string; no normalization, no locale tailoring
Whitespace removed: no space after ':' or ','
Integers 1,2,3 serialized by ES6 Number::toString, unchanged
Output is UTF-8, no BOM, no trailing newline
Sorting is recursive over every object at any depth, including objects that are elements of arrays
Array element order is preserved verbatim — arrays are never reordered or re-sorted
Inner object {"y":1,"x":2} → {"x":2,"y":1} by code-unit sort (x=0x0078 < y=0x0079)
Outer object keys: "a" < "z" (0x0061 < 0x007A)
Literals true/false/null emitted lowercase, no whitespace anywhere
Same structural nesting as input; only key order changes
n1 (1e21): ES6 Number::toString uses exponential notation when the decimal exponent is >= 21 → "1e+21" (explicit '+', minimal exponent digits, no leading zeros/'+' on the mantissa beyond '1')
n2 (1e-7): exponential when the value is < 1e-6 → "1e-7" (exponent not zero-padded)
n3 (0.000001 = 1e-6): 1e-6 is at the threshold, so fixed notation is used → "0.000001" (ES6 switches to exponential only for exponents < -6)
n4 (100000000000000000000 = 1e20): 1e20 < 1e21, so fixed notation → "100000000000000000000" (no exponent, no digit-grouping)
n5 (-0): RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3 mandates negative zero be serialized as "0" (no minus sign); matches ES6 Number::toString(-0)
n6 (333333333.33333329): shortest round-trip decimal for the IEEE-754 double → "333333333.3333333" (16 significant digits; 333333333.33333329 and 333333333.3333333 denote the same double)
General: JS-style ES6 number formatting only — never printf/exponential-always, never trailing ".0" for integral values
Keys n1..n6 already in code-unit order, so only number formatting changes here

"aa" precedes "ü" because the first differing code unit is 0x0061 (97) vs 0x00FC (252) and 97 < 252 — per-code-unit comparison, not locale collation (a locale collator would place ü next to u, after aa alphabetically differently)

"€" sorts last: U+20AC is a single BMP code unit 8364, greater than 0x00FC; (note: for non-BMP characters the surrogate unit 0xD8xx-0xDFFF would sort before U+E000-U+FFFF, which is why JCS specifies UTF-16 units rather than code points)
Non-ASCII characters are NOT \u-escaped: keys and values are emitted as literal UTF-8 ("ü" = C3 BC, "€" = E2 82 AC)
No whitespace; string values unescaped/literal
s1: U+000A uses the two-character short escape \n, not \u000a (RFC 8785 §3.2.2.2 / ES JSON.stringify)
s2: U+0009 uses the short escape \t
s3: U+0022 (quote) escaped as \" ; backslash U+005C would be \\ ; these are the only non-control characters ever escaped
s4: U+00E9 (é) emitted literally as UTF-8 C3 A9 — JCS never applies \u escaping to non-ASCII, and never uses \u for BMP characters

s5: the two non-rendering characters are read as C0 controls U+0001 and U+001F, escaped as lowercase-hex \u0001 and \u001f; only \b \f \n \r \t have short forms, all other U+0000–U+001F use \u00xx with lowercase hex digits
Escaping set is exactly: " , \ , and U+0000–U+001F; U+0020 (space), U+007F (DEL) and all non-ASCII pass through unchanged
Keys s1..s5 already sorted, so compact and JCS coincide for this case apart from the (identical) escape rules

data.weakest_point: Case 5, key "s5": I cannot see the raw bytes of the two non-rendering characters in "control  " and assumed they are C0 controls U+0001 and U+001F, giving "control\u0001\u001f". The rule in doubt is which characters actually occupy those two positions: JCS escapes only U+0000–U+001F (with \b \f \n \r \t short forms, otherwise lowercase \u00xx) and leaves everything >= U+0020, including U+0020 spaces, U+007F and all non-ASCII like U+00A0/U+200B, unescaped as literal UTF-8. If those two positions are literal spaces (0x20) the correct value is "control  " with no escapes at all; if they are a space plus one control char it is "control \u00xx". Everything else (code-unit key ordering, recursive array-nested sorting, ES6 number formatting incl. 1e+21 / 1e-7 / 0.000001 / -0→0 / 333333333.3333333, and literal UTF-8 passthrough) I verified computationally.
